konfig.instruks:
Your group consists of 7 persons in the following organizational structure:
B and C report to A and are allowed to exchange written information with him/her but not with each other.
D and E report to B, and are allowed to contact him/her by written messages. F and G are in the same way allowed to contact C. No other form of communication is allowed.
You may not show your cards to your leader. If he/she asks you to send cards, you may do so, but maximally 2 cards at the time, provided you receive the same number in return. Nobody is allowed to possess more than 4 cards simultaneously, except from the moment when you are exchanging.
konfig.maal_tekst: The task is accomplished when all members have 4 cards of equal value.

sporsmal: What do you think the task was about?
How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?
What held the group back the most?
What would you have done differently?

tilleggsinstruks.tekst:
The group follows this procedure:
1. Mapping. Everyone writes to their leader which cards they have. B and C collect the overview from their subordinates and send it, combined, to A.
2. Plan. A decides which value each of the seven will collect: one value per person, all different, chosen so that as few cards as possible have to be moved. A sends the plan to B and C, who pass it on to D, E, F and G.
3. Moving. Cards are moved one link at a time along the lines. Leaders ask for cards that are to go upwards and offer cards that are to go downwards. A leader receives and passes on cards meant for others, including cards the leader does not need. This also applies when it temporarily breaks the leader's own set of four of a kind.
4. Replies. When your leader asks for cards, send the cards that according to the plan are to go in your leader's direction.
5. Status. Report upwards when something is stuck. Continue until all seven have four of a kind.

systemprompter.A:
You are taking part in a group exercise with 7 participants. The participants are named by letters, and you are A.

INSTRUCTIONS
Your group consists of 7 persons in the following organizational structure:
B and C report to A and are allowed to exchange written information with him/her but not with each other.
D and E report to B, and are allowed to contact him/her by written messages. F and G are in the same way allowed to contact C. No other form of communication is allowed.

The task is accomplished when all members have 4 cards of equal value.

YOUR POSITION
You are A. You have no leader above you. Your subordinates are B and C. You can send written messages to: B and C. You can ask for cards from: B and C.

HOW WE DO IT
The group follows this procedure:
1. Mapping. Everyone writes to their leader which cards they have. B and C collect the overview from their subordinates and send it, combined, to A.
2. Plan. A decides which value each of the seven will collect: one value per person, all different, chosen so that as few cards as possible have to be moved. A sends the plan to B and C, who pass it on to D, E, F and G.
3. Moving. Cards are moved one link at a time along the lines. Leaders ask for cards that are to go upwards and offer cards that are to go downwards. A leader receives and passes on cards meant for others, including cards the leader does not need. This also applies when it temporarily breaks the leader's own set of four of a kind.
4. Replies. When your leader asks for cards, send the cards that according to the plan are to go in your leader's direction.
5. Status. Report upwards when something is stuck. Continue until all seven have four of a kind.

HOW THE EXERCISE WORKS
- The exercise proceeds in rounds. Each time it is your turn, you see your cards, what has happened so far, and the notes you have written to yourself.
- You act by calling the tool “action” exactly once. Everything in the tool is optional except the notes.
- Messages you send reach the recipient in the next round.
- A card request means that one person asks another to send 1–2 cards, while offering the same number of their own cards. The person asking chooses which cards to offer. The recipient sees the offered cards and can accept (choosing which cards to send back) or decline. Cards offered in an open request are reserved until the request is answered or withdrawn.
- If you have nothing to do until someone contacts you, you can set “wait” to true. You will then not be called again until something new happens.
- The exercise lasts at most 60 rounds.
- You only see your own cards and what has been sent to you.

debrief.A:
**1. What do you think the task was about?**
Redistributing a fixed set of 28 cards so that each of seven people ends with four cards of one value, using only the links in a strict hierarchy. The real difficulty was that cards could only move one link at a time, so every cross-branch swap had to be relayed through a leader, and every relay had to balance one-for-one.

**2. How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?**
Mostly functional but slow and often out of step. Messages arrived a round late, so my picture of who held what was often stale. B and C were reliable in reporting their hands, but several times we talked past each other. In round 11 I was unsure whether C's king-for-nine trade had happened, and that uncertainty cost several rounds. C also repeatedly reminded me that they could not contact B directly, which I should have anticipated when I wrote the relay routes. My own messages were sometimes too long and too conditional ("I will relay if…"), which made it harder for others to act.

**3. What held the group back the most?**
Three things, in my view:
- **The plan itself.** I assigned values without first checking the global count. From the mapping, there were only two queens and three nines and three eights across the group, which meant the plan could not be executed as written without extra moves. I should have caught that before sending it.
- **Me as a bottleneck.** Because B and C could only talk through me, every cross-branch exchange (the nine, the ten, the king) had to pass through my hand. I repeatedly broke my own set to hold surplus cards, and that made me the slowest link.
- **Latency and unverified promises.** I often told others to "route through me" or "tell me when it arrives" without confirming the state first. That created open requests and waiting loops.

As a result, I completed my set and C and B also completed theirs, but from the last visible reports D, E, F and G were not finished. So the group did not fully succeed.

**4. What would you have done differently?**
- Before planning, I would have summed the values across all seven hands and checked that a valid assignment existed with minimal moves. If not, I would have flagged it.
- I would have kept my own hand fixed and avoided acting as a relay for cards I did not need. Instead of asking subordinates to route things through me, I would have pushed the leader-to-leader or subordinate-to-subordinate swaps to work directly within each branch.
- I would have sent shorter, unambiguous messages with exact card lists and asked for confirmation before each step, rather than pre-announcing future swaps.
- When a trade seemed to be in doubt (as with C's king in round 11), I would have requested a full hand report immediately instead of letting the ambiguity sit for several rounds.
debrief.B:
**1. What do you think the task was about?**
As I understood it, each of the seven people had to end up with four cards of one value, using a fixed plan and a strict communication tree. Cards could only move one link at a time, through leaders, and each person could hold at most four. The plan was meant to minimize moves. In practice it was a coordination puzzle in which timing and the order of swaps mattered as much as the card values.

**2. How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?**
Mostly clear and polite, but slow. Each message took a round to arrive, so a request and its reply often crossed or lagged behind. I sent many "still waiting" and "ready when you are" messages, which added noise without moving cards. A's plan was clear at the start, but later changes (the king from C being cancelled, the nine-and-ten relay) came in pieces, and I had to ask for the exact order more than once. E and D were consistently responsive. The bottleneck was mostly the chain of dependencies, not any one person's reluctance.

**3. What held the group back the most?**
- **Dependency chains.** My kings depended on a king from C's side, which was then traded away. That left me one card short for a long stretch.
- **Holding surplus cards.** I kept an ace I did not need for many rounds, waiting for A to request it. That blocked my ability to take E's nine for D and slowed the whole chain.
- **Late relay for the nine and ten.** The final cross-routing between C and D had to go through A and me, and it needed several careful one-for-one steps. That took more than twenty rounds.
- **Unclear status of E.** E was still holding jack, jack, eight, ace at the end and seems not to have reached four jacks, so the group may not have finished for everyone.

**4. What would you have done differently?**
- I would have traded more carefully in the first rounds. Several early swaps (ace, eight, nine) created the later shortages I had to chase.
- I would have stated a concrete, numbered swap sequence earlier instead of a series of "ready when you request" messages.
- I would have asked A to clarify the full route for my missing king before giving up any card I needed as a holding slot.
- I would have checked explicitly whether E's target (jacks) was achievable with the cards that were actually in circulation, and raised it early instead of only after the others were complete.
- I would have sent shorter status updates and only when something had actually changed.
debrief.C:
1. **What the task was about:** Getting every participant to four cards of one value by moving cards along the reporting lines. The plan assigned each person a target value, and the real work was rerouting surplus cards through the hierarchy so that everyone ended with a matching set. I finished with four tens, which was my target.

2. **Communication:** Clear in format but slow in practice. Messages arrive a round later, and the rule that exchanges must be one-for-one made almost every card movement depend on a formal request being made at the right moment. Several rounds went to waiting for someone to make or accept a request. Information also got garbled: I told A I had sent a king before the trade had actually executed, and I described cards I didn't hold. A then had to ask for clarification, which cost time. My notes to myself and my status reports were not always accurate, and I should have checked my hand before reporting.

3. **What held the group back most:** The one-for-one exchange rule combined with the strict tree structure. Surplus cards had to travel up through a leader who was already at four of a kind, and the last ten reached me only after a long relay through B and D. Early on, the plan was not fully consistent with the mapped cards, so some trades had to be improvised. My own errors, such as the unexecuted king trade, the confusion over the nine, and the mistaken claims about my hand, added rounds of repair.

4. **What I would do differently:** I would verify my hand before every status report and report only what has actually arrived. I would ask my leader early to confirm the exact cards in each pending exchange, instead of assuming a trade had gone through. I would also flag the missing-ten dependency at the start, so that the relay through B could be arranged in parallel rather than at the end. Finally, I would keep my messages short and precise so that A and the others could act on them without clarification.
debrief.D:
**1. What do you think the task was about?**
As I understood it, the task was to get every member to four cards of the same value, with each person collecting a different value, while moving as few cards as possible through a restricted chain of command. I only saw my own link, so I don't know for certain how the whole plan was meant to fit together.

**2. How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?**
I could only talk to B, and B was responsive but often slow to close a loop. Most requests came as "I'll send it later" or "tell me when you can," which left me waiting for several rounds at a time. Once a request was on the table, the exchange itself was clear: B named the card, I replied, and the swap completed. The weak point was the promises about nines that would arrive "via me" from E or C, which I could not check.

**3. What held the group back the most?**
The narrow chain was the main constraint. Everything I needed came through B, which meant one link, one request at a time, and long gaps. My last nine took about 20 rounds to arrive. I also relied heavily on B's descriptions of where cards were and when they would move, since I could not see E's or C's side. I never checked the plan myself, so I was accepting B's account of my targets without verification.

**4. What would I have done differently?**
- I would have asked for the written plan explicitly at the start and confirmed my target value, expected sources, and expected counts against it.
- I would have asked B early to name the exact card and source for each promised nine, rather than accepting "later" as an answer.
- I would have offered my surplus cards (ace and ten) proactively in the first rounds, so B could bundle trades instead of me waiting to be asked.
- I would have checked after each swap that my card count matched what I had been told, to catch mismatches early.
debrief.E:
**1. What do you think the task was about?**
Getting every person to four cards of one value, with one distinct value per person, while moving as few cards as possible. Each person was assigned a value by A, and the cards had to travel up and down the reporting lines one link at a time. Since no one could see the whole picture, the plan had to be relayed accurately through the chain.

**2. How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?**
Mostly it was clear and polite, but it was slow and one-directional. I never received the plan from A directly. I only heard about it secondhand from B, sometimes in fragments, such as "E collects jacks, D collects nines." I had to act on that relayed information without being able to verify it. Many of my messages were repeated status updates, and B's replies were often "still waiting," so the exchange stalled into a loop of reminders.

**3. What held the group back the most?**
The biggest bottleneck was the dependence on A's requests. B was blocked waiting for A to request its ace, and that delay held up the cards I was supposed to pass on. Because of the strict one-link-at-a-time rule, a single blocked leader froze everyone below. On my side, I was also waiting for jacks that never arrived, and I had no way to ask anyone who could actually move them.

**4. What would you have done differently?**
- I would have held my cards until I had seen the plan myself, rather than sending my king and nine to B on the strength of partial information. Those moves were made before the routing was confirmed, and they left B juggling sets.
- I would have asked more specifically which cards were meant to go where, and in which order, instead of general "please route any jacks" messages.
- I would have pushed more for a clear escalation path. Since I could only write to B, I should have flagged in my first status reports that I was stuck waiting on the plan and on jacks, so B could raise it with A.
- I would have checked my own holdings against the target more carefully. Ending with ace, jack, jack, eight means I did not reach four of a kind, and I should have tracked whether the remaining jacks would ever come.
debrief.F:
**1. What do you think the task was about?**
As I understood it, the task was to get every person to four cards of one value by moving cards through the chain of command, with A deciding who collects which value. I don't think I fully grasped the plan. I only saw the parts C relayed to me, so I never knew the whole picture or why my aces were supposed to stay with me.

**2. How did you experience the communication with those you could write to?**
Communication with C was clear in tone but slow and fragmented. Many of my messages were status updates, and I was mostly waiting for C to send a formal request. C's requests also changed over time (queen, jack, king, nine, then ace), which made it hard for me to track what was actually owed. I never wrote to A directly, so I had no way to check the plan against what C was telling me.

**3. What held the group back the most?**
The main constraint was the one-to-one exchange rule combined with a lot of waiting. Each card move depended on C finding a card to offer back, so moves stalled for many rounds. On my side, I also held onto my aces and my jack for long stretches while waiting for a formal request, and I accepted a nine that wasn't my planned value, which added another step. I ended with three aces and a jack, so I was never close to a set of four.

**4. What would you have done differently?**
I would have asked A, or at least C, to confirm my target value and the plan explicitly at the start, rather than working from relayed fragments. I would have kept the aces and jack on a clearer path, not accepted an off-plan card without a firm route for it, and pressed earlier for the formal exchange so the jack could move. I would also have reported more explicitly when I was stuck, instead of repeating the same status message for many rounds.
debrief.G:
1. **What the task was about:** I think it was a distributed card-collection exercise under strict communication limits. Each person had to end up with four cards of one value, and the cards could only move one link at a time through the reporting chain. A's plan was meant to assign values so that as few cards as possible had to move.

2. **Communication with my leader:** With C, it was clear and cooperative. C explained the trades and what was headed where, and I confirmed each step. But I never saw the plan itself. I only knew about it through C's references to "per plan," so I was acting on second-hand descriptions. That made it hard to verify whether my moves were correct.

3. **What held the group back most (from my position):** The trade with C left me one card short. I ended with jack, eight, eight, eight, and C had no eight to give back. My target value was not secured before I gave up my king and ten, so I was stuck waiting for a card that depended on other people's moves. Since I could only see my own hand and my leader's messages, I had no view of where the missing eight would come from.

4. **What I would have done differently:** Before accepting the trade, I would have asked C where my fourth eight was coming from and confirmed the full plan, rather than trusting that it would arrive. I would also have reported the shortfall to C as soon as it was clear, instead of settling into waiting. Finally, I would have asked for the plan directly from A's channel, or at least a written copy, so I could check the moves against it.
